Hatchlings of the slow worm emerge from the parchment-shelled egg after a period of intra-ovarian development, and at birth they display a snout–vent length averaging 4.872 centimeters [Lb = 4.872 centimeters]. This modest neonatal size, which corresponds to a wet body mass of only 0.549 grams [Wwb = 0.549 grams], reflects the substantial yolk reserves that sustain the embryo up to the moment of parturition. The delicate nature of these hatchlings, with their reduced limb remnants and elongated, serpentiform trunk, makes them particularly vulnerable to desiccation and predation during their first weeks of terrestrial life. Comparative studies within the family Anguidae indicate that such a small SVL at hatching (4.872 centimeters) [Lb = 4.872 centimeters] is typical of species that give birth to large litters of fully formed young, a reproductive strategy that trades greater offspring number for reduced individual size. In the weeks following emergence, these young-of-year reptiles embark on a period of rapid mass gain, consuming small invertebrates such as slugs and earthworms, which provide the protein necessary for skeletal growth and the accumulation of lipid reserves that will sustain them through their first winter brumation.

As the slow worm progresses through its juvenile phase, individuals gradually approach the size threshold that marks the onset of reproductive activity. For females, the onset of puberty is reached at a snout–vent length of 13.5 centimeters [Lp = 13.5 centimeters], a developmental milestone that typically coincides with the achievement of roughly two-thirds of the ultimate adult size. This SVL at puberty (13.5 centimeters) [Lp = 13.5 centimeters] is not attained uniformly across the population; rather, it reflects the interplay of local thermal conditions, food availability, and individual growth trajectories. In populations occupying cooler, high-latitude sites, females may require an additional growing season to reach this critical size, whereas individuals in more productive lowland habitats can achieve pubertal status more rapidly. The attainment of this body length signals the initiation of gonadal activation, with the ovaries beginning to produce yolked follicles. Once puberty is reached, females become capable of contributing to the next generation, although first reproduction is often deferred until the following breeding season to allow for the full development of the reproductive apparatus and the accumulation of sufficient energy reserves.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the age at which slow worms achieve their first reproductive event has been documented at 2.5 years after birth [tR = 2.5 years after birth]. This extended interval from birth to first reproduction is characteristic of a relatively slow life-history strategy, wherein energy is preferentially channeled into somatic growth and maintenance rather than early reproductive output. At the same thermal regime of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], maximum lifespan has been recorded at 54 years [am = 54 years], a remarkably long duration for a small squamate reptile and one that underscores the species' capacity for delayed senescence. The pronounced discrepancy between the age at first reproduction (2.5 years after birth) [tR = 2.5 years after birth] and the potential longevity (54 years) [am = 54 years] suggests that slow worms enjoy an extended reproductive window spanning several decades at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C] at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. Longitudinal mark-recapture studies in central European populations have corroborated these laboratory findings, revealing that individuals can survive for multiple decades under natural conditions, though most wild animals likely succumb to predation or environmental stressors well before reaching physiological senescence.

Females that have attained a body length of approximately 16.8 cm exhibit a wet body mass averaging 13.8 grams , a value that represents the typical mass–length relationship for reproductively active individuals. At this body size and under the same thermal conditions of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the reproductive output of adult females has been characterized as roughly 6.88 offspring per year [Ri = roughly 6.88 offspring per year]. This annual reproductive rate must be interpreted as the total number of live-born young produced across one full breeding season, as slow worms are viviparous and give birth to fully developed neonates rather than depositing eggs. The production of roughly seven young per year [Ri = roughly seven young per year] at a maternal mass of 13.8 grams  represents a substantial energetic investment when one considers the costs of gestation, which in a cool-temperate ectotherm can extend over several months. This fecundity is comparable to that reported for other anguid lizards of similar body size and likely reflects a constraint imposed by the limited abdominal volume available for carrying developing embryos during the prolonged gestation period.

The relationship between body size and fecundity in this species is further illuminated by the observation that females can eventually reach a maximum snout–vent length of 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters], though few individuals attain this ultimate size in the wild due to extrinsic mortality. A female slow worm approaching this asymptotic length would possess substantially greater abdominal capacity than a younger, smaller conspecific, and as a result she would be capable of producing larger litters. However, the estimated annual reproductive output of approximately 6.88 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 6.88 offspring per year] is derived from individuals of average body mass, not from these exceptional large adults. Across its geographic range, the slow worm exhibits considerable variation in asymptotic body size, with mainland European populations generally producing larger females than those on offshore islands, a pattern often attributed to differences in predation pressure and resource seasonality. The maximum longevity of 54 years [am = 54 years] recorded in captivity under temperature-controlled conditions provides an extreme benchmark for life-history studies, yet it is important to note that wild individuals rarely survive beyond two decades, the discrepancy being largely attributable to the cumulative risks of predation, habitat disturbance, and food limitation in natural environments at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C].
